title: Constipation After Drinking Alcohol: Causes, Relief, Prevention
excerpt: Why alcohol can leave you constipated the next day, why some people get diarrhea instead, what actually gets things moving, and when to see a doctor.
metaDescription: Constipated after drinking? Why alcohol backs you up, how long it lasts, what helps get things moving, how to prevent it, and when to see a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** constipation after drinking is common, usually temporary, and almost always clears up within a day or two once you rehydrate, eat normally, and get back to your usual routine. Alcohol doesn't constipate everyone. Plenty of people get the opposite problem. But a mix of dehydration, a disrupted gut, the food you ate (or didn't eat), poor sleep, and a broken daily rhythm can easily leave you backed up the morning after, or for a couple of days after a big weekend. This guide explains why it happens, why some people get constipation while others get diarrhea, what actually helps, and the signs that mean it's worth calling a doctor.

**The quick fixes:** drink water steadily through the day (not all at once), eat something with fiber and some fat, have your usual coffee if you tolerate it, go for a walk, and give yourself unhurried time on the toilet after a meal. If you're still stuck after two or three days, a gentle over-the-counter option such as a fiber supplement or an osmotic laxative is reasonable for most healthy adults. Skip the "hair of the dog." More alcohol makes the underlying dehydration worse.

> **When to see a doctor.** Occasional constipation after a night out is normal. But get medical advice promptly if you have **severe or worsening belly pain**, a **swollen, hard belly**, **vomiting** (especially if you can't keep fluids down), **no bowel movement and no gas** for more than a couple of days, **blood in your stool** or **black, tarry stools**, a **fever**, or **unexplained weight loss**. See a doctor too if constipation lasts more than a week or two, keeps coming back, or is a new change in your bowel habits, especially if you're over 45. Severe belly pain after heavy drinking can also signal pancreatitis, which needs urgent care. If you or someone else is very confused, can't stay awake, or is vomiting repeatedly after drinking, call 911 or go to the emergency room. This article is general information, not medical advice.

## Why Alcohol Can Make You Constipated

There isn't one single cause. Alcohol affects your gut in several ways at once, and the result depends on how much you drank, what you drank, what you ate, and how your own digestive system tends to behave. Here are the main drivers.

### 1. Dehydration pulls water out of your stool

This is the biggest and best-understood factor. Alcohol suppresses **vasopressin**, also called antidiuretic hormone. Vasopressin's job is to tell your kidneys to hold on to water. When alcohol turns it down, your kidneys release more water as urine, which is why you end up making so many trips to the bathroom while drinking.

By the next morning, many people are mildly dehydrated. When your body is short on water, your large intestine (colon) does what it always does with incoming waste: it absorbs water from it. With less water to spare, it pulls more out. Stool becomes drier, harder, and slower to move. That's the classic "hard and difficult to pass" constipation many people notice after drinking.

If you want the full picture of how alcohol affects your fluid balance, see our guide to [whether alcohol really dehydrates you](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-dehydrate-you).

### 2. Alcohol changes how your gut moves

Your gut moves food along with waves of muscle contractions called peristalsis. Alcohol interferes with this rhythm, but not always in the same direction. Research on alcohol and gut motility is mixed. In some people and at some doses, alcohol speeds parts of the gut up, which is one reason diarrhea is so common after drinking. In others, it slows things down. Heavy, long-term drinking has also been linked to changes in how the gut muscles and nerves work.

The practical takeaway: alcohol makes your digestion less predictable. If your system tends to run slow anyway, a night of drinking can tip it further in that direction.

### 3. The food you ate (and the food you skipped)

Nights out don't usually come with a balanced, high-fiber dinner. Think about what tends to happen:

- **Greasy, low-fiber late-night food**: pizza, burgers, fries, white bread, cheese. These are filling but low in the fiber that keeps stool soft and moving.
- **Skipping meals**: some people don't eat much before or during drinking. Less food in means less bulk to trigger a normal bowel movement.
- **A next-day "hangover diet"**: plain toast, crackers, white rice, and salty snacks are easy on a queasy stomach but low in fiber.

Fiber matters because it holds water in your stool and adds bulk, both of which help your colon move it along. A day or two of low-fiber eating is enough on its own to slow some people down, before alcohol even enters the picture.

### 4. Your routine gets thrown off

Bowels like routine. Many people have a fairly regular time of day when they go, often in the morning after waking and eating. A late night, a lie-in, a skipped breakfast, travel, or sleeping somewhere unfamiliar can all disrupt that rhythm. Ignoring the urge to go, which is easy to do when you're out or not at home, also lets stool sit longer in the colon, where more water gets absorbed.

### 5. Poor sleep

Alcohol may help you fall asleep, but it disrupts sleep later in the night. Your gut has its own daily rhythm that is tied to your sleep-wake cycle. A short or broken night can throw that off. If you also struggle to sleep after drinking, our guide on [why you can't sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking) explains what's going on.

### 6. Medications you took alongside

This one is easy to overlook. Several common medicines can cause constipation, and people often reach for them after a night out:

- **Antihistamines** used as sleep aids (such as diphenhydramine in many "PM" products)
- **Anti-nausea medicines** such as some forms of meclizine or dimenhydrinate
- **Antacids containing aluminum or calcium**, such as some forms of Tums. If you rely on these for post-drinking heartburn, our guide on [Tums and alcohol](/never-hungover/tums-and-alcohol) covers what to know.
- **Iron supplements**
- **Opioid painkillers** and some prescription medicines

Mixing sedating medicines with alcohol is a bad idea for other reasons too, since they add to each other's drowsiness. If you take a prescription that causes constipation, ask your pharmacist how alcohol fits in.

## Why Some People Get Constipation and Others Get Diarrhea

If your friends are complaining about the opposite problem, you're not imagining things. Diarrhea is actually the more commonly reported bowel complaint after drinking. Both can happen, sometimes in the same person on different nights, or even one after the other.

The difference comes down to which effects win out:

| Tends toward diarrhea | Tends toward constipation |
|---|---|
| Alcohol speeding up the gut | Dehydration drying out stool |
| Large volumes of fluid, especially beer | Spirits with little mixer and little water |
| Sugary mixers and sweet drinks | Low-fiber food and skipped meals |
| Irritation of the gut lining | Disrupted routine and ignoring the urge |
| Greasy food in people sensitive to fat | Constipating medicines |
| Tendency toward loose stools or IBS-D | Tendency toward slow transit or IBS-C |

Some people get a "rebound" pattern: loose stools during or right after drinking, followed by a day or two of nothing as their gut recovers and they're still dehydrated. That's also normal. If loose stools are your issue, see our guide on [diarrhea after drinking](/never-hungover/diarrhea-after-drinking).

## Does the Type of Drink Matter?

There's no strong research ranking drinks by how constipating they are, so be wary of anyone who claims a definitive list. What we can say:

- **Spirits with little or no mixer** deliver alcohol with very little water. If you don't drink water alongside, you can end up more dehydrated than you'd expect.
- **Beer** brings a lot of fluid along with the alcohol, and it's more often linked to loose stools and bloating than constipation. Still, the alcohol in beer suppresses vasopressin just like any other drink.
- **Red wine** contains tannins, which some people find mildly binding. The evidence on this is thin, and it doesn't affect everyone.
- **Cocktails and sugary mixers** are more often associated with diarrhea in people sensitive to sugar, but they don't protect you from dehydration.

The amount you drink and how much water you have alongside it matter far more than the type.

## How Long Does Constipation After Drinking Last?

For most healthy people, it clears up within **one to three days**. Once you rehydrate, eat some fiber, sleep properly, and get back into your normal routine, your bowels usually follow.

It's also worth knowing that "normal" varies a lot. Going anywhere from three times a day to three times a week can be normal for healthy adults. Missing one day after a night out isn't constipation in itself. What matters is a change from your own usual pattern, and whether you feel uncomfortable, bloated, or have to strain.

If it's lasting longer than a few days, or this happens after almost every time you drink, that's a sign to look at the bigger picture. That might mean how much you're drinking, or an underlying gut condition worth discussing with a doctor.

## What Helps: How to Get Things Moving Again

Start with the simplest steps. Most people won't need anything beyond the first few.

### Rehydrate steadily

Water is the foundation. Sip regularly through the day rather than gulping a liter at once. Your body absorbs fluid better that way, and you're less likely to feel sick. If you feel washed out or have also had diarrhea or vomiting, an electrolyte drink can help you hold on to fluid more effectively. Our guide on [how to rehydrate after drinking](/never-hungover/how-to-rehydrate-after-drinking) covers what to drink and how much.

Warm drinks can help too. Many people find that a warm drink in the morning helps trigger a bowel movement.

### Eat fiber, and pair it with water

Once your stomach can handle it, aim for foods that bring both fiber and water:

- **Prunes or prune juice.** Prunes contain fiber plus sorbitol, a natural sugar alcohol that draws water into the bowel. They have been tested in clinical trials for constipation with good results, and they're one of the better-supported food remedies.
- **Kiwifruit.** Several studies have found that eating two kiwis a day can help people with constipation. It's a gentle option.
- **Pears, apples, and berries**, ideally with the skin on.
- **Oats, whole-grain bread, and bran cereal.**
- **Beans, lentils, and chickpeas**, though these can cause gas in some people.
- **Vegetables**, especially leafy greens.

One caution: if you don't usually eat much fiber, don't suddenly load up on it. A big jump in fiber without enough water can make bloating and discomfort worse. Add a little more than usual and keep drinking water.

### Don't forget some healthy fat

A little fat with a meal can help trigger the natural "gastrocolic reflex," which is your colon's tendency to contract after you eat. Foods like eggs, avocado, nuts, or a drizzle of olive oil count. This isn't a license for more greasy takeaway, which is low in fiber. Think balanced meal, not fries. If you're wondering about breakfast specifically, see our guide on [eggs for a hangover](/never-hungover/eggs-for-hangover).

### Coffee, if you tolerate it

Coffee stimulates the colon in many people, often within a short time of drinking it. That's why a morning coffee works as a reliable trigger for lots of people. Caffeine also has a mild diuretic effect, but for regular coffee drinkers this is small, and a cup or two is unlikely to dehydrate you meaningfully. Just don't let coffee replace water. If coffee upsets your stomach or makes hangover anxiety or a racing heart worse, skip it.

### Move your body

Gentle movement helps your gut move. A 15 to 30 minute walk is one of the simplest and most effective things you can do. You don't need a hard workout, and exercising hard while dehydrated and hungover isn't a great idea anyway.

### Give yourself time on the toilet

A few practical tips that genuinely help:

- **Go when you feel the urge.** Don't put it off.
- **Try after a meal**, especially breakfast, when the gastrocolic reflex is strongest.
- **Raise your feet on a small step or stool** so your knees are higher than your hips. This position straightens the angle of the lower bowel and makes it easier to pass stool without straining.
- **Don't strain hard or sit for ages.** Prolonged straining can lead to hemorrhoids or small tears. If nothing happens after about 10 minutes, get up and try again later.

### Over-the-counter options

If you're still stuck after two or three days despite water, fiber, and movement, over-the-counter products are reasonable for most healthy adults. Read the label and follow the dosing instructions.

| Type | Examples | How it works | Good to know |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bulk-forming fiber | Psyllium (Metamucil), methylcellulose (Citrucel) | Adds bulk and holds water in stool | Gentle, but works over a day or more. Must be taken with plenty of water. |
| Osmotic laxative | Polyethylene glycol (MiraLAX), magnesium hydroxide (milk of magnesia) | Draws water into the bowel to soften stool | Usually works within one to three days. Magnesium products aren't suitable for people with kidney problems. |
| Stool softener | Docusate (Colace) | Helps water mix into stool | Mild. Evidence that it works well on its own is limited. |
| Stimulant laxative | Senna, bisacodyl (Dulcolax) | Makes the bowel muscles contract | Works faster, often overnight. Can cause cramping. Best for occasional short-term use. |

Some practical points:

- **For a one-off post-drinking slowdown, start gentle.** Fiber or an osmotic laxative is usually plenty.
- **Stay hydrated while using any laxative.** Laxatives that draw water into the bowel work better, and are safer, when you're drinking enough.
- **Don't rely on laxatives regularly** without talking to a doctor. If you find you need them after every night out, it's worth a conversation.
- **Check with a pharmacist** if you're pregnant, have kidney or heart problems, or take other medications.

## What About Bloating, Gas, and Cramps?

Constipation and bloating often travel together. When stool sits in the colon longer, gut bacteria have more time to ferment it, which produces gas. Alcohol itself can also irritate the stomach and gut lining, and carbonated drinks like beer and mixers add gas of their own. The result can be a swollen, tight, uncomfortable belly.

Usually this eases as things start moving again. Walking, warm drinks, and avoiding more carbonated drinks for a day all help. Puffiness in your face is a different issue, mostly linked to fluid shifts and inflammation, which we cover in our guide to [alcohol face bloating](/never-hungover/alcohol-face-bloating).

A dull, crampy discomfort that eases when you pass gas or stool is typical of constipation. Pain that is **severe, constant, sharp, or getting worse**, especially in the upper belly and spreading to your back, is not. That kind of pain needs medical attention. Our guide to [stomach pain after drinking](/never-hungover/stomach-pain-after-drinking) explains the different types of pain and what they can mean.

## What Your Stool Is Telling You

A quick look before you flush can tell you a lot. Hard, lumpy stool that's difficult to pass points to dehydration and low fiber, which is the typical post-drinking pattern. Very loose stool points the other way.

Color is worth noting too. Dark stool can come from iron supplements, bismuth products such as Pepto-Bismol, or dark foods. But **black, tarry, sticky stool or red blood** can signal bleeding in the gut, and that needs a doctor promptly, especially after heavy drinking. Our guide on [poop color after drinking](/never-hungover/poop-color-after-drinking) goes through the colors and what they mean.

## How to Prevent Constipation Next Time

You can't control everything about how your gut reacts to alcohol, but you can stack the odds in your favor:

1. **Eat a proper meal before drinking.** Ideally one that includes some fiber, protein, and fat. Drinking on an empty stomach makes most morning-after problems worse. See our guide on [drinking on an empty stomach](/never-hungover/drinking-on-an-empty-stomach).
2. **Alternate alcoholic drinks with water.** A glass of water between drinks slows your drinking down and limits dehydration.
3. **Drink a big glass of water before bed**, and keep one by the bed.
4. **Choose a better late-night snack** if you can. Something with a bit of fiber beats a pile of fries.
5. **Eat breakfast the next day.** Even something small helps trigger your gut's morning rhythm.
6. **Keep up your usual fiber intake** over the weekend, not just on weekdays.
7. **Be mindful of sleep aids and antacids** that can be constipating, and avoid combining sedating medicines with alcohol.
8. **Drink less.** This is the least exciting tip and the most effective. Most morning-after symptoms, constipation included, scale with how much you drank.

## Regular Drinking and Your Gut

If you only get constipated after the occasional big night, that's very normal and not a sign of anything serious. If you drink most days, though, it's worth knowing that alcohol has longer-term effects on the gut.

Research has linked regular heavy drinking to changes in the gut microbiome (the community of bacteria living in your intestines), a leakier gut lining, and altered gut motility. These changes can show up as ongoing bowel problems in either direction: constipation, diarrhea, bloating, or a mix. Our guide on [how alcohol affects your gut microbiome](/never-hungover/how-alcohol-affects-your-gut-microbiome-the-hidden-health-impact-2025) goes deeper on this.

People with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) often find that alcohol is a trigger. If you have IBS and notice that drinking reliably sets off symptoms, cutting back or keeping a simple diary of what you drank and how you felt can help you spot patterns.

If you notice that your bowel habits have changed in a lasting way, don't just put it down to drinking. A persistent change in bowel habits is something a doctor should look at, regardless of the cause.

## When Constipation Isn't Just a Hangover Symptom

Most post-drinking constipation is harmless and short-lived. But constipation can occasionally be a sign of something more serious, or a symptom that needs medical care. Go back to the "when to see a doctor" box at the top of this page if you're unsure. In short, the red flags are:

- Severe, constant, or worsening belly pain
- A swollen, hard, or very tender belly
- Vomiting, especially if you can't keep fluids down
- No bowel movement and no gas passed for several days
- Blood in your stool, or black, tarry stools
- Fever, or feeling very unwell
- Unexplained weight loss
- Constipation that lasts more than a week or two, or keeps coming back
- A new, lasting change in your bowel habits, especially if you're over 45 or have a family history of bowel cancer

These signs don't mean something serious is definitely going on. But they're worth getting checked rather than waiting out.

## Can Supplements Help?

There's no supplement that specifically prevents constipation after drinking. The things with the best track record are the simple ones covered above: water, fiber, movement, and a regular routine. A fiber supplement such as psyllium is the most useful "supplement" here, and probiotics have mixed evidence for constipation in general.

Some people also take hangover supplements to help with how they feel the morning after more broadly. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of that research comes from animal and lab studies, with limited human data, so it's promising rather than proven. There is no good evidence that DHM prevents or treats constipation, and it doesn't replace drinking water or eating well. If you want to try it for general morning-after support, popular picks include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. For the habits with the best evidence overall, see [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

## The Bottom Line

- Constipation after drinking is common and usually clears up within one to three days.
- The main cause is dehydration, since alcohol makes your kidneys release more water and your colon then pulls more water out of your stool. Low-fiber food, skipped meals, poor sleep, a disrupted routine, and some medicines add to it.
- Some people get diarrhea instead, or both one after the other. Both are normal responses to alcohol.
- Water, fiber, a balanced breakfast, coffee if you tolerate it, a walk, and unhurried time on the toilet fix most cases.
- If you're still stuck after two or three days, a fiber supplement or osmotic laxative is a reasonable next step for most healthy adults.
- See a doctor for severe belly pain, a swollen belly, vomiting, blood or black stools, fever, no gas for days, or constipation that lasts or keeps coming back.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why does alcohol make me constipated?**

The main reason is dehydration. Alcohol suppresses vasopressin, the hormone that tells your kidneys to hold on to water, so you lose more fluid as urine. The next day your colon pulls extra water out of your stool, leaving it hard and slow to pass. Low-fiber food, skipped meals, poor sleep, a disrupted routine, and constipating medicines such as some antihistamines and antacids add to the effect.

**How long does constipation after drinking last?**

For most healthy people it clears up within one to three days once they rehydrate, eat some fiber, sleep properly, and get back to their normal routine. If it lasts more than a week or two, keeps coming back, or is a new lasting change in your bowel habits, see a doctor.

**Why do I get diarrhea some nights and constipation others?**

Alcohol affects the gut in several ways at once. It can speed up parts of the gut and irritate the lining, which pushes toward diarrhea, while dehydration, low-fiber food, and a disrupted routine push toward constipation. Which effect wins depends on how much you drank, what you drank and ate, and how your gut tends to behave. Some people get loose stools first and then a day or two of constipation as they recover.

**What is the fastest way to relieve constipation after drinking?**

Start with water sipped steadily through the day, a breakfast with some fiber and a little fat, your usual coffee if you tolerate it, and a 15 to 30 minute walk. Then give yourself unhurried time on the toilet after eating, with your feet raised on a small stool. Prunes or prune juice are a well-supported food option. If nothing has happened after two or three days, a fiber supplement or an osmotic laxative such as polyethylene glycol is reasonable for most healthy adults.

**Is it safe to take a laxative after drinking?**

For most healthy adults, an occasional over-the-counter fiber supplement or osmotic laxative used as the label directs is reasonable once the alcohol has cleared. Drink plenty of water with it, since dehydration is usually part of the problem. Magnesium-based products aren't suitable for people with kidney problems, and you should check with a pharmacist if you're pregnant, have heart or kidney conditions, or take other medications. If you need laxatives after most nights out, talk to a doctor.

**Does beer or liquor cause more constipation?**

There's no strong research ranking drinks by how constipating they are. Spirits with little mixer deliver alcohol with very little water, so they can leave you more dehydrated if you don't drink water alongside. Beer brings more fluid and is more often linked to loose stools and bloating. How much you drink and how much water you have alongside it matter far more than the type of drink.

**When should I see a doctor about constipation after drinking?**

Get medical advice promptly for severe or worsening belly pain, a swollen or hard belly, vomiting, no bowel movement and no gas for several days, blood in your stool or black tarry stools, fever, or unexplained weight loss. Severe upper belly pain after heavy drinking can signal pancreatitis and needs urgent care. Also see a doctor if constipation lasts more than a week or two or keeps coming back.

**Can DHM help with constipation after drinking?**

There is no good evidence that DHM prevents or treats constipation. DHM is a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver, mostly in animal and lab studies with limited human data. For constipation, the simple steps work best: water, fiber, movement, and getting back to your normal routine.
